bp: A social media video is not just a block of text with moving pictures attached. It can contain spoken words, captions, on-screen text, visual symbols, named people or groups, and background references that make a phrase harmful in one setting and harmless in another. This paper serves the moderation setting where a platform must decide whether a video carries hate or toxic content, but also must explain what evidence led to that decision. The need appears before any model is named: a removal or warning is a public judgment about speech, and a black-box score is hard to audit. The paper therefore treats hateful video analysis as an evidence-management problem. The system must collect clues from frames, audio, text, and context, keep them inspectable, and show whether they support, contradict, or fail to contribute to the final judgment.
wh: The hard part is that the harmful meaning may not live in one channel. A transcript can look mild while a visual cue changes its meaning. A frame can show an object whose significance depends on speech or outside context. On-screen text may identify the target, while audio supplies the hostile claim. If a system simply blends all channels into one hidden description, it may produce a correct label without any usable reason, or it may hide the fact that one channel was missing. Deployment makes that worse because moderators, users, and auditors need to know whether the decision came from a phrase, a detected object, a named entity, a background reference, or agreement across sources. The paper also has to handle conflict: different channels may point in different directions, and treating conflict as ordinary noise loses important information.
naive: A smart beginner would train a supervised classifier on labeled hate-video datasets and ask it to output hateful or not hateful for each video. That is natural because the abstract says many current approaches already do this, and benchmark accuracy is easy to measure. The failure is that a single final label does not say what evidence mattered. Another beginner might concatenate frame features, transcript text, and contextual features, then let a model learn a combined score. That can improve prediction, but it still buries the reasoning. If the model flags a video because a named entity appears near toxic words, or because visual and audio cues agree, the fused representation may not expose that path.
ap: The paper's central move is to keep evidence separate long enough for it to be inspected. Instead of treating visual, audio, textual, and contextual information as ingredients melted into one feature soup, the system turns each source into explicit evidence records. From frames it extracts object detections and on-screen text. From audio it extracts speech transcripts. From text it extracts toxicity scores and named entities. From a fixed offline retrieval corpus it adds contextual information. These pieces are placed into a shared evidence structure, then ordered by a deterministic ranking mechanism. The ranking emphasizes semantic contribution: which clue actually changes the meaning of the case. It also records cross-modal agreement and conflict, and it marks absent or non-contributing channels as null rather than pretending every channel spoke.
mech: The mechanism begins with one video. The visual path samples frames and records concrete findings: detected objects and text visible on the screen. The audio path turns spoken content into a transcript. The text path then analyzes available words, including speech and on-screen text, for toxicity scores and named entities, so the system can track both harmful tone and who or what is being discussed. A contextual path searches a fixed offline corpus for background material relevant to the video, which matters when a phrase, entity, or symbol needs outside context to be interpreted. All of these outputs are stored in a shared evidence structure rather than immediately collapsed into one score. Next, a deterministic ranking mechanism prioritizes evidence by semantic contribution. In plain terms, it asks which pieces most affect the meaning of the decision, which pieces repeat the same story across channels, and which pieces disagree. If a channel has no useful signal, it is marked as null so absence is represented explicitly. The final decision then passes through an orchestration layer. The system can use a fully deterministic baseline, or it can call a constrained large language model reasoner for cases where richer reasoning is wanted. The fallback guarantees mean the pipeline still has a defined behavior if the optional reasoner is unavailable or unsuitable.
math: The main mathematical idea is evidence scoring under uncertainty. Each extracted clue becomes a small item that can be counted, compared, ranked, or ignored. Ranking means deciding which clues should be inspected first because they contribute more to the final meaning. Here, better evidence is not merely a louder signal; it is evidence that changes the interpretation of the video in a semantically relevant way. Agreement is another mathematical object: if visual text, speech, and retrieved context point to the same harmful target or claim, their convergence is stronger than any one clue alone. Conflict is also represented, because disagreement between channels is not the same as missing data. The null marker is a simple but important modeling choice: it separates silence from negative evidence. Retrieval adds similarity: the system compares the video's entities or content against a fixed offline corpus and brings back context that appears related. The optional language model reasoner uses constrained generation, meaning its free-form explanation is bounded by the evidence structure and fallback rules. The tradeoff is accuracy versus auditability: the system gives up some unrestricted end-to-end blending so the path from clue to judgment can be inspected.
dots: This paper sits inside the repo's multimodal vision-language family, where the shared problem is deciding how images, words, sound, timing, and context should cooperate without erasing the useful details of each channel. It is especially close to the misinformation and trust family because the final question is not only whether content is harmful, but whether the supporting evidence can be shown and checked. It also connects to ranking: the system sorts evidence by contribution before it asks for a final judgment. It connects to retrieval because outside context comes from a fixed corpus rather than from the video alone. Nearby hate and social-content papers in the repo examine live-stream routing, hateful memes, implicit hate, cultural moderation, and evidence-grounded explanations. This paper's branch is video-focused evidence attribution: it asks how a moderation system can say not just what it decided, but which visual, audio, textual, and contextual clues made the decision defensible.
ww: The approach should work better than the naive classifier because it matches the shape of the problem. Hate-video meaning is often compositional: one cue identifies a group, another expresses hostility, and another supplies context. A model that collapses everything early can learn shortcuts, such as treating a recurring word, object, or entity as harmful without checking how it is used. Keeping sources independent slows that collapse. The system can notice that two channels support the same interpretation, that one channel contradicts another, or that a channel contributes nothing. Deterministic ranking helps because the same evidence receives the same priority each time, which matters for auditing. The shared evidence structure gives the optional language model reasoner a grounded workspace: it reasons over extracted clues rather than inventing a story from the raw video prompt alone. The fallback layer reduces dependence on that optional reasoner by preserving a deterministic path. The abstract's evaluations on HateMM, ImpliHateVid, and manually annotated YTHate are consistent with testing whether this evidence-centered structure helps on both established and newly annotated hateful video cases.
po: The payoff is a hateful-video analysis system whose output can be inspected. Instead of only returning a prediction, it can expose the objects, on-screen text, transcripts, toxicity cues, named entities, retrieved context, and cross-modal agreements or conflicts that shaped the decision. That makes the system more useful for deployment settings where moderators must justify actions and auditors must check whether the system relied on sensible evidence. The abstract grounds the evaluation in HateMM, ImpliHateVid, and a manually annotated YTHate dataset, so the claimed capability is tied to multimodal hate-video analysis rather than generic toxicity detection.
limits: The approach assumes the extractors are reliable enough: object detection, on-screen text reading, speech transcription, toxicity scoring, named-entity extraction, and retrieval can all make mistakes. A fixed offline corpus improves control, but it may omit new slang, events, or cultural references. Deterministic ranking is auditable, yet it depends on the chosen definition of semantic contribution. Marking absent channels as null is useful only if absence is detected correctly. The optional language model reasoner may make explanations more flexible, but the abstract does not prove that every generated reason faithfully caused the final decision. The reported datasets do not prove behavior across every platform, language, culture, or adversarial video style.
